analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic refuge, offshore waters, and oil shale lands to oil and gas drilling, with royalty shares for conservation.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a single senator with no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Energy Committee and died there without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would end federal bans on oil and gas leasing across wide areas of federal land and water: it lifts the moratoria on offshore drilling, opens part of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain to a leasing program, and removes limits on commercial oil shale development on public land. It also repeals a rule barring federal agencies, including the military, from buying synthetic fuels that create more greenhouse gas emissions than regular gasoline. To balance that, it routes half of the new drilling royalties into dedicated accounts for conservation programs and renewable energy, plus 3% to low-income home energy assistance.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain access to drill on public lands and waters long off-limits, including the Arctic refuge coastal plain and previously withdrawn offshore areas, and oil shale developers could get a commercial leasing program. Alaska would receive 27% of new federal drilling revenue. Energy conservation and renewable energy programs would gain a dedicated funding stream from royalties, and low-income households would benefit from a 3% share for home energy assistance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies and Alaska

how_it_helps.text: It authorizes a competitive oil and gas leasing program in the Arctic refuge coastal plain, with a first lease sale of at least 200,000 acres required within 22 months of enactment [S3].
It revokes presidential and statutory withdrawals of offshore submerged lands from leasing and repeals the Gulf of Mexico moratorium, opening those areas to exploration and production [S2,S3].
It removes the prohibition on issuing final regulations and holding lease sales for commercial oil shale development on public land [S2,S3].

Half of new lease revenues go into a Conservation Reserve Account and a Renewable Energy Reserve Account to fund efficiency programs, clean energy research, and job training, with 20% to debt reduction and 3% to the low-income home energy assistance program [S3].

The bill imposes a 16.5% minimum royalty, a 2,000-acre surface footprint cap, seasonal drilling limits to protect caribou calving, reclamation liability on lessees, and project labor agreement requirements on ANWR leases [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Protected public lands and waters would lose their protected status: the Arctic refuge coastal plain, previously withdrawn offshore areas, and parts of the Gulf of Mexico would be opened to drilling, with risks to fish, wildlife, and subsistence resources there. The bill also shortcuts environmental review for the ANWR program, limiting the alternatives the Interior Department must analyze and the public comment window to 20 days. Repealing the synthetic fuel procurement ban would let federal agencies buy higher-emission alternative fuels.
analysis.who_pays_short: Protected lands, coastal communities, and wildlife

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the prohibition on oil and gas production from the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and declares drilling there compatible with the refuge's purposes without further findings, while limiting the required environmental review to a preferred action and a single alternative and a 20-day public comment window [S3,S2].

It repeals the Energy Independence and Security Act ban on federal agencies procuring alternative or synthetic fuels with higher lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions than conventional petroleum, reopening federal demand for higher-carbon fuels [S2,S3].

Price relief would be slow: the first ANWR lease sale could not happen for at least 22 months after enactment, and offshore exploration and development would take years more before any production reached the market [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a large transfer of public resources to energy producers with real money for conservation and renewables, funded only if drilling revenue actually materializes. Its environmental safeguards are unusually detailed for a drilling bill, but it shortcuts the normal review process in the most sensitive area it opens and could delay any effect on prices for years. Weighing whether opening the Arctic refuge and offshore waters is worth those trade-offs is exactly the judgment Congress never made, because the bill never came to a vote.

outcome.mechanism: One senator introduced it in October 2008, nobody signed on, the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee never took it up, and it expired when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. George Voinovich introduced the bill on October 1, 2008 and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S5,S1].
The committee took no further action, and the bill received no floor vote before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5,S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Arctic refuge coastal plain, withdrawn offshore areas, and oil shale lands stayed off-limits to leasing, and the federal synthetic fuel procurement ban stayed in force; oil and gas companies gained nothing from it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Protected lands stayed protected; drillers gained nothing

for.name: Sen. George Voinovich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks, then saw it referred to committee; he recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Senate committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Jeff Bingaman, D-NM)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 1, 2008 and took no further action on it; no hearing, markup, or floor consideration followed.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no cosponsor joined, so no partisan split can be measured; the single sponsor was a Republican and the committee that held the bill was run by Democrats.

industries.note: The bill hands drillers access to the Arctic refuge coastal plain, previously withdrawn offshore waters, and the Gulf areas under moratorium, on public land the industry could not otherwise lease. Its interest in expanded access conflicts with protecting those areas, though royalty sharing would also route 53% of new revenue to conservation, renewable energy, and low-income energy aid.

industries.industry: Oil shale and tar sands developers
industries.note: The bill repeals the appropriations rider blocking final commercial leasing regulations and lease sales for oil shale on public land, opening a new resource to industry. Environmental groups had sought to keep that program on hold pending further study.

industries.industry: Synthetic and alternative fuel producers, including coal-to-liquids
industries.note: Repealing the Energy Independence and Security Act procurement ban would let federal agencies, including the Defense Department, buy synthetic fuels even when their lifecycle emissions exceed conventional petroleum. The ban's purpose had been to keep federal demand from supporting higher-carbon fuel.

industries.industry: Renewable energy and energy efficiency sectors
industries.note: Half of new drilling royalties would flow into reserve accounts to fund efficiency programs, clean energy research and deployment, and related job training. The funding is contingent on drilling revenue actually being collected.

industries.industry: Alaska Native corporations and North Slope local governments
industries.note: The bill conveys land to the Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and Arctic Slope Regional Corporation and creates a $35 million annual impact aid fund for North Slope communities, while also exposing the coastal plain, homeland of the Kaktovikmiut Inupiat, to development the communities would then have to manage.
